book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know

chapters.file: ch03 - Tom Petty and Philosophy We Need to Know.md

chapters.relation: Luke Dick argues Petty is the best American rock and roll ever produced because his simple songs distill the American everyperson: the person in Indianola longing to leave a crummy town, the arrival in Hollywood finding it a sham. He contrasts Petty's effortless accessibility with the density of Dylan and Springsteen, and identifies Petty's signature move as making futility fun, a smart-assed drawled defiance heard in "American Girl" and "Mary Jane's Last Dance." The foreword frames the whole volume as a communion of fans trying to understand Petty from another lens, warning that the chapters will be hard pressed to beat Petty's own simplicity.

Section introduction to the ethics chapters, framed by Petty’s October 2017 death: it argues his real achievement was working to be timeless — the shelved 1982 outtake “Keep a Little Soul” sounding native in 2018 — and that he “lived what he believed,” chasing dreams despite guaranteed heartache, refusing to explain his songs, and standing up to record-company executives. It closes by describing Petty’s political thought as “a deontology that puts duty to the fans first,” invokes Nietzsche as appreciating the gesture of turning the volume up rather than snoozing through the Reagan years, and sketches the volume’s five philosophical “buds”: epistemology, aesthetics, ontology, and two ethics chapters on the outcast and heartbroken as redeemable antiheroes of the everyday.

Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.

chapters.file: ch11 - 2. Echoes of Past and Present.md
chapters.relation: Crippen and Dixon treat the album Echo, written during Petty's divorce, heroin use and severe depression, as organized by crisis and reversion: its lyrics and productions compulsively echo earlier eras of his life, from 1950s TV westerns and his abusive father in "About to Give Out" to the Jeff Lynne years and Wildflowers in "Accused of Love" and "Echo." They invoke Freud and Lacan's psychoanalytic account of trauma repetition, where the past is relived in hope of a different outcome and sublimated into art. The album's sparse, energy-conserving repetition is then read through Nietzsche's will-to-power cycle, in which merely holding on is symptomatic of illness, yet the closing "One More Day, One More Night" and the album's very creation exemplify Nietzschean health as strength to expand against obstacles, since we possess art lest we perish of the truth.

chapters.file: ch12 - 3. Don’t Come Around Here, Mary Jane.md
chapters.relation: Auxier narrates three moments of Petty's video era (1979 Damn the Torpedoes, 1985, 1993) through Bataille's "general economy": living beings reduced to things can only be redeemed by wasting, sacrifice and death, which explains why the band devouring Alice in "Don't Come Around Here No More" and the morgue assistant dressing, dancing with and floating out Kim Basinger's corpse in "Mary Jane's Last Dance" are creepy yet somehow ordered rather than gratuitous. He argues MTV inverted the economy of music judgment so images became the cart pulling the horse, and reads Petty's top-hat ringmaster and the recurring circles of the videos as the ring of the sacred and profane where the accursed share of excess energy is spent. Phenomenology of the "creepy" is his method for seeing what MTV shows us but we prefer not to know.

chapters.file: ch13 - 4. Tom Petty and the Meaning of Life.md
chapters.relation: Innes reads Petty through The Birth of Tragedy: Petty fuses Dionysian frenzy (the Oakland Coliseum "Makin' Some Noise" crowd as communal creation) with Apollonian form, and his refusal of genres, synthesizers and the hit-factory gives life the creative meaning Nietzsche demands. Jeff Lynne and ELO are cast as the contemporary Wagner, Socratic and Apollonian producers of pleasant ditties like "Don't Bring Me Down" that lack access to tragedy. Petty's "Trailer" models Greek tragedy (impulse as hamartia foreclosing freedom), while his lawsuits against MCA and The Last DJ dramatize the tragic bind that free musical expression needs the very industry that restrains it.

Auxier practices phenomenological description, naming each Heartbreaker by the feel of his look ("LoverBen," "BlondieMike," "RedneckRamone") and analyzing a sausage-ball expectation violation, to show how the band's sound sold them before their incongruous visuals did. He traces quotationalism and obsessive circle imagery through the videos (the Abba quotation and virtual kiss in "Here Comes My Girl," the wedding-ring cake of "Yer So Bad"), and reconstructs how Petty rejected Mike Campbell's "Boys of Summer" demo because it did not feel like the present, while Don Henley, neutralizing anticipation and just hearing it, turned the same chord circle into the song's refusal of self-destroying nostalgia. Petty's criterion of "feel" emerges as a phenomenological talent that can miss the future without misreading the present.

Edwards reads "Insider" as an attack on the assumption that lovers have privileged access to the beloved's mind: its narrator rages not at the betrayal but at himself for failing to foresee it. With Beauvoir's "The Woman in Love" she diagnoses the lovers' delusion of merged consciousness, noting it grips women harder under patriarchy, which is why Stevie Nicks rightly refused the song as "not a woman's song." Frye's contrast between the arrogant eye (projection without self-knowledge) and the disciplined, searching loving eye explains the narrator's journey, while Ratcliffe's radical empathy accounts for his final gamble of imagining her "quiet world of white and gold," pointing toward Beauvoir's authentic love founded on recognizing the other's freedom.

Volpert argues Tom Petty was a feminist, the only classic-rock male whose catalog consistently grants women rational equality and agency, adopting Susan McClary's feminist New Musicology as her lens and marching through Greatest Hits song by song. She reads the forced removal of the Lolita cover from "American Girl," the consensual, threat-free request of "Breakdown," and "Listen to Her Heart" as Petty's reply to Ike Turner's cocaine-locked party, and defends "You Got Lucky" as a conceit about band technology rather than misogyny. The chapter confronts the gaze directly, arguing "Here Comes My Girl" watches a woman walking toward you as formidable rather than objectified, with the video's flirtations redirected homoerotically at the Heartbreakers themselves.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know.md
chapters.relation: Zelinski and Fallis chart Petty's epistemic arc. His early songs ("I Need to Know," "Fooled Again," "Shadow of a Doubt") crave certainty about lovers' fidelity, a Desmond-free obsession closest to Descartes' quest for certainty beyond doubt, except Petty's problem is other minds, not the external world, and his trust that eyes directly reveal feeling sides with Moore's common-sense perception; Sartre's "hell is other people" names why another free person's future love can never be certain. From Full Moon Fever onward ("Into the Great Wide Open," "Time to Move On," "Learning to Fly") Petty instead embodies Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment and the Buddha's "don't know mind" and Daoist farmer's "we'll see," finding tranquility in uncertainty, craving nothing, flying with eyes open.

Watkins takes the recurring road image ("Runnin' Down a Dream," "Kings Highway," "Learning to Fly") as a probe of whether the future is open. Against determinism and Aristotle-style fatalism she argues from lived experience: we cannot feel our choices as unfree, and even a determined world would remain unpredictable, so Petty's open road wins. His optimism in "It'll All Work Out" needs no faith in a good outcome, only the passing of time under our feet, and persistence then becomes an Aristotelian virtue required for eudaimonia, a duty owed to the kind of beings we are, and Sartrean authenticity in which Petty made himself through his project of rock'n'roll.

Auxier names Petty the master of "liminal moments" when something is finally seen for what it is (the betrayed lover's realization behind "You Got Lucky," the unknown pain of "American Girl"), then stages the 1929 Davos debate between Cassirer's humane, Goethe-reading phenomenology and Heidegger's Angst before the abyss, being-toward-death, and the "moment of vision." He indicts Heidegger's Nazism and betrayal of Husserl as what "Petty-ness," the asshole-beast crouching in everyone's darkdeepdown, becomes when it wins, contrasting Petty's public apology for the Confederate flag and his cease-and-desist to George W. Bush. The chapter ends with the unguarded Petty smile as "Here Comes My Girl" made philosophy, an instance of authentic being-with-others that Heidegger declared impossible.

Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.

chapters.file: ch24 - 12. When Money Shouldn’t Be King.md
chapters.relation: Berkey reconstructs Petty's two industry battles, the bankruptcy gambit to void the contract sold along with Shelter Records and the month-long standoff against MCA's $9.98 superstar pricing, then reads The Last DJ as Petty's considered position on the business of music. He argues Petty rejected subjectivism about music's value: because listeners can be mistaken about the value of their own enjoyment, a formal argument shows executives like "Joe" who program only what profits act wrongly, even if consumers willingly pay. "Money Becomes King" completes the critique, showing how profit-focus degrades the fan's quasi-religious concert experience and corrodes Johnny's motivation to make valuable music at all.

Hakli challenges the "one man's war" image of Petty using Bratman's shared agency and Tuomela's we-mode theory of group agents and collective commitment. He reinterprets the MCA contract and price fights as actions of a group: the Heartbreakers as a band with Petty as benevolent dictator, plus lawyers, manager Elliot Roberts who paid the bills, roadie Bugs Weidel who drove the master tapes around California, and the fan write-in campaign against the price hike. The difference between Petty and the corporate guy is only the size of the "we" each acts for; Petty's we-mode stretched to everyone who loves rock'n'roll.

chapters.file: ch26 - Part V How to Rebel.md
ch27 - 14. Anything that’s Spiked Is Fine.md
chapters.relation: Volpert asks where rebellion lives, in the lone guitarist or the listening group, using Hardt and Negri's claim that a rebel's true opposite is not failure but co-option, i.e. selling out. Arendt's distinction between totalitarian and authoritarian systems models the music industry as authoritarian (creativity permitted so long as profit at the top goes unchallenged), and her banality-of-evil analysis of Eichmann prompts the question of whether there is a banality of rebellion. Petty's satirical puppetry of authority voices in "Century City" and the silent spiked-collar punk of "Spike," kin to Bartleby and James Dean, show that individuals can rebel against authoritarian packs while groups, even the Heartbreakers, only ever drift into authoritarianism.

Luft reads Petty's apology for flying the Confederate flag as the awakening of justice, the Platonic cardinal virtue and Aristotle's common-good virtue, and asks what is worth defending. Socrates refusing escape in the Crito, Jesus, Njal's saga and Harry Potter exemplify self-sacrificial refusal to defend oneself for a higher ideal, the model Petty aspires to in "I Won't Back Down." Through Royce, Fletcher and Keller on loyalty, the Confederate "clueless rebels" are diagnosed with misplaced loyalty: regional pride is ethical only when we hold something as ours because it is right, never as right because it is ours.

chapters.file: ch29 - 16. I Should Have Known It.md
chapters.relation: Watkins reads the later albums Mojo and Hypnotic Eye ("Power Drunk," "Burnt Out Town," "Playing Dumb," "Shadow People") through Clifford's ethics of belief: the powerful suppress their doubts like the unseaworthy shipowner and come to sincerely believe their own lies, while the overpowered hide behind the cliche that everyone is entitled to an opinion. Because belief formation is a doing inseparable from action, there is a moral obligation to hold beliefs to evidentiary standards, we should have known, and James's will-to-believe and fideist appeals (Tertullian, Pascal, Kierkegaard) offer no license for self-serving faith. Facing the evidence in front of us is the first step to telling the power-drunk it is the last time they are going to hurt us.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Meditation of St. Thomas (Petty).md

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: Marxist literary theorist who analyzed postmodernism as the cultural logic of late capitalism, marked by pastiche, the erasure of high/low art, and depthlessness.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire framework for reading Petty's music and persona as postmodern is built on Jameson's account of pastiche, commodified history, and 'free-floating' affect.

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of the 'general economy': excess energy that must be wasted, sacrifice, the accursed share, and the sacred/profane boundary of thinghood.
holes.why: Chapter 12 reads Petty's videos 'Don't Come Around Here No More' and 'Mary Jane's Last Dance' entirely through Bataille's economy of waste, sacrifice and the creepy.

holes.name: Matthew Ratcliffe
holes.what: Phenomenologist of mood and existential feelings who distinguishes everyday empathy from 'radical' empathy that refuses to presuppose a shared world.
holes.why: Chapter 16 leans on Ratcliffe's radical empathy and existential feelings to explain how the narrator of 'Insider' finally understands his beloved.

holes.name: Authentic Love (Beauvoir)
holes.what: Beauvoir's ideal of love founded on the reciprocal recognition of each lover's freedom rather than fusion, delusion, or possession.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues 'Insider' charts a move from the lovers' mind-reading delusion toward exactly this Beauvoirian authentic love.

holes.name: The Arrogant Eye and the Loving Eye
holes.what: Frye's contrast between a presumptuous seeing that projects one's own mind onto others and a disciplined, self-knowing, loving attention.
holes.why: Chapter 16 uses Frye's arrogant/loving eye distinction, not her birdcage model, as the central tool for interpreting 'Insider'.

holes.name: Susan McClary
holes.what: Feminist musicologist of the New Musicology who analyzes how music constructs gender through lyrics and composition (Feminine Endings).
holes.why: Chapter 17 explicitly adopts McClary's feminist music analysis as the framework for reading Petty's Greatest Hits catalog as feminist.

holes.name: Ernst Cassirer
holes.what: Neo-Kantian philosopher of symbolic forms and humane humanism, Heidegger's opponent in the 1929 Davos debate.
holes.why: Chapter 21 stages Petty's 'change of heart' against the Cassirer-Heidegger Davos confrontation and holds up Cassirer's decency as the anti-asshole ideal.

holes.name: Assholes: A Theory
holes.what: Aaron James's account of the asshole as someone who consciously and self-servingly exempts himself from rules he knows apply to everyone else.
holes.why: Chapter 21 builds its moral (try not to be an asshole) and its indictment of Heidegger directly on James's definition.

holes.name: Objectivism vs Subjectivism about Value
holes.what: The debate over whether value (here, of music) consists only in listeners' subjective enjoyment or partly in mind-independent properties people can be mistaken about.
holes.why: Chapter 24 argues Petty held a partially objectivist view of music's value, which grounds his ethical critique of profit-maximizing record companies.

holes.name: We-Mode and Shared Agency
holes.what: Theories (Tuomela, Bratman) of group agency, joint action, and collective commitment in which individuals act for group reasons rather than purely personal ones.
holes.why: Chapter 25 reinterprets Petty's legal battles with MCA as we-mode group action of the Heartbreakers rather than lone-hero individualism.

holes.name: Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri
holes.what: Political theorists of Empire (2000) who analyze how global capitalist systems co-opt and absorb rebellion.
holes.why: Chapter 27 opens with Hardt and Negri's thesis that co-option (selling out), not failure, is the rebel's true opposite.

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American idealist philosopher of community and loyalty who held that genuine loyalty is to ideals and expresses itself as justice (The Philosophy of Loyalty, 1908).
holes.why: Chapter 28 grounds its account of Petty's misplaced-then-corrected Confederate loyalty in Royce's philosophy of loyalty.

holes.name: William K. Clifford
holes.what: Author of 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877), the evidentialist thesis that it is wrong always to believe anything on insufficient evidence, illustrated by the shipowner.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses Clifford's shipowner and ethics of belief as the core framework for Petty's 'Power Drunk' and 'Playing Dumb' critique of self-deception.
